title: From conventional steels to high-entropy alloys: progress in the design of high-performance structural materials
abstract: Abstract 3d late transition metal (3dLTM) medium-entropy and high-entropy alloys (MEAs and HEAs, respectively), also known as multiprincipal element alloys or complex concentrated alloys, have emerged as one of the most actively developing and technologically versatile branches of current metallic materials research. Among various HEA families, Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C systems and their subsystems offer a good combination of structural flexibility and tunability of phase composition. These relatively lightweight alloys bridge high-Mn steels with MEAs/HEAs and other complex concentrated solid-solution materials. This review provides an integrated analysis of recent progress in 3dLTM HEAs with a specific emphasis on compositional optimization by late 3d transition metals, using classical production routes from industrial steel precursors, and a design strategy originating from the Fe-rich corner of phase diagrams, for achieving high mechanical strength combined with tensile ductility. The mechanisms controlling microstructural evolution under plastic deformation and subsequent strengthening are also evaluated.   Modern compositional design, classical heat treatment and deformation processing,  short-range ordering, and phase transformation engineering are connected into processing–structure–property relationships. The analysis reveals that Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C-based systems HEAs show highly transformable  microstructure and good ability for deformation-induced strengthening, while retaining a reasonable tensile plasticity. These features provide useful control over mechanical properties, enabling exceptional combinations of tensile strength (1.5–2 GPa), tensile ductility (4–15%), and Vickers hardness (> 5 GPa), depending on chemical composition, structure and processing conditions. The paper outlines emerging opportunities in alloy design, advanced thermomechanical processing and structure engineering for next-generation structural HEAs and MEAs.

sections.heading: General introduction
paragraphs: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), also conceptualized as multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), or compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) with nearly equiatomic compositions [ 1 ,  2 ], as well as a closely related group of medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) [ 3 ,  4 ], have evolved into one of the most transformative classes of metallic materials exhibiting good mechanical properties [ 5 ,  6 ], especially for some applications [ 7 ,  8 ], good catalytic activity [ 9 ] and biological properties [ 10 ].

Phase stability in any alloy depends on the Gibbs free energy rather than entropy alone. The thermodynamic design of high-entropy alloys is governed by the interplay between enthalpy, entropy, and structural parameters that control solid-solution stability, which are closely connected with the Hume-Rothery rules for the formation of solid solutions [ 11 ]. Structural stability is further constrained by atomic size mismatch, which must be minimized to avoid excessive lattice strain, and by electronegativity difference, where large values favor compound formation over solid solutions [ 12 ]. A useful criterion is the Gibbs free energy of mixing (Δ G mix ), where negative values indicate thermodynamic phase stability. The mixing enthalpy (Δ H mix ) should remain close to zero, for strongly negative values favor intermetallic compound formation, while positive values promote phase separation. In contrast, a high mixing entropy (Δ S mix ) affects Δ G mix  and stabilizes single-phase solid solutions. The dimensionless thermodynamic parameter  Ω  =  T Δ S mix /Δ H mix  describes the competition between entropic solid solution stabilization ( T Δ S mix ) and enthalpic interactions (Δ H mix ). High values of  Ω  indicate dominance of entropy-driven solid-solution formation. According to the location of the elements in the periodic table, the crystal structure of HEAs is effectively predicted by the number of electrons in the outer shell – outer shell electron concentration (OSEC), where low OSEC favors BCC/cI2 (early transition metals—ETMs) and high OSEC stabilizes FCC (late transition metals—LTMs). Intermediate values may lead to dual-phase (BCC + FCC/cF4) structures, but possible ordering often happens owing to large Δ H mix  between ETMs and LTMs. Here one should mention that electronic and magnetic entropy contributions can reach up to 50% of the configurational entropy and play a crucial role in phase stability by causing significant variations in entropy differences among phases [ 13 ]. One should also note that the non-regular solid-solution problem [ 14 ] creates an issue as well.

Traditional HEA design uses the middle of the compositional space of the phase diagrams. The first generation of HEAs focused on equiatomic alloys designed to maximize configurational entropy, such as the classical Cantor alloy with an equiatomic FeMnCoNiCr composition (the absence of the molar/atomic fractions in the chemical composition indicates the equimolar/equiatomic composition). This alloy combines high ductility at room temperature, strong work hardening due to dislocation activity and nano-twinning as well as exceptional fracture toughness at cryogenic temperature [ 5 ,  15 ,  16 ]. This unusual combination of low-temperature toughness and ductility made it scientifically and technologically attractive. The high chromium content further contributes to its excellent corrosion resistance [ 17 ].

Thus, technologically important FCC HEAs are composed primarily of chemically similar elements, usually 3d late transition metals (3dLTMs) such as Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu [ 18 ,  19 ]. Some of them form a dual-phase FCC + BCC structure. Nevertheless, some compositions may exhibit atomic ordering [ 20 ], including the formation of σ phase [ 21 ,  22 ] and short-range order [ 23 ,  24 ]. Al and Ti additions increase mechanical strength by ordering BCC cI2 into cP2 structure [ 25 ,  26 ] or precipitation of nanoscale coherent L1 2 -Ni 3 (Ti, Al) precipitates and L2 1 -(Ni, Co) 2 TiAl intermetallic compounds on aging between 700 and 800 °C [ 27 ]. Nb [ 28 ], V [ 29 ,  30 ] additions produce nearly similar effects. And although energy often wins over entropy when an element having a strongly negative mixing enthalpy with the others is added [ 31 ,  32 ], the HEA term is nowadays well established in scientific literature.

More than two decades of research established that core HEA concepts, that is high configurational entropy, crystal lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion [ 33 ], though still questioned in many cases [ 34 ], and other effects, provide combinations of structural simplicity but chemical complexity not attainable in traditional alloy design.

sections.heading: Examples of HEAs developed from the corners of phase diagrams.
paragraphs: While the earliest HEAs utilized the LTM FCC [ 1 ,  2 ] and refractory ETM BCC solid solutions [ 19 ], recent developments have shifted focus toward practical [ 35 ], non-equiatomic compositionally asymmetric HEAs [ 18 ], including alloys engineered from specific corners of phase diagrams.

Here, corner-approach high-entropy alloys (CA-HEAs) are defined as non-equiatomic MEAs/HEAs designed by starting from an optimized conventional alloy base, such as Fe–Mn–Al–C steel, and progressively expanding compositional complexity while preserving an optimal phase-composition and properties. In this context, Fe-based alloy systems, particularly those related to steels, offer a unique advantage. Among 3d LTMs, steels have a long and well-established history, with a deep understanding of their phase transformations, deformation mechanisms, and mechanical processing routes. This knowledge provides a strong foundation for the development of new HEA series. By combining the concept of compositional complexity with the rich metallurgical background of steels, it becomes possible to design alloys with improved mechanical properties.

Thus, it quickly became clear that high-entropy alloys can be generated not only via compositional optimization of equiatomic alloys [ 36 ,  37 ] but also through aluminum enrichment of conventional industrial Fe–Mn–Al–Si–C steels up to 11 and 22.5 mass% [ 38 ,  39 ]. For example, an Fe–20Mn–1.2 C alloy with 11 mass% Al showed yield strength of about 1000 MPa and > 40% ductility [ 38 ]. C is the main alloying element of steel, and it well dissolves in the FCC phase stabilizing it. The addition of C to the Fe 20 Mn 20 Cr 20 Ni 20 Co 20  alloys (here the subscript indicates atomic/molar percentages) induces solid-solution strengthening [ 40 ].

A well-known family of high-Mn-content Fe–Mn–Al–C steels [ 41 ,  42 ] is widely reviewed in several works [ 38 ,  43 ]. These alloys demonstrate high ultimate strength values ranging from 500 to 1200 MPa and large tensile ductility reaching 80% and more and demonstrate high hardening ability [ 44 ]. Thus, lightweight Fe–Mn–Al–C steels are a logical starting material for producing HEAs and MEAs as a base system [ 45 ], because they already contain up to ~ 40% of the solute content. The Fe–Mn–Co–Al–C [ 46 ], Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Al–C [ 47 ] and Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C [ 48 ] system alloys have been developed by the approach from the Fe-rich corner of a multicomponent phase diagram as indicated in Fig.  1 . The alloys were produced by deviating from the boundary towards equiatomic composition to obtain optimal mechanical properties. This idea worked out because the corner composition already possesses good mechanical properties, while incremental 3dLTM additions still can utilize classical strengthening mechanisms, including solid-solution strengthening and  κ -carbide precipitation and ductilization by transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) behavior [ 49 ]. Also, relatively simple processing (forging, rolling) is retained. This approach leads to optimized MEA/HEA compositions with balanced strength and ductility. These alloys were found to have: a single-phase FCC solid solution with dislocations-mediated strengthening effect at high Mn content; complex duplex (FCC + BCC) structures at high Al content and possible precipitation of nano-size  κ -carbide (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC in the FCC phase [ 50 ,  51 ] on aging at the intermediate temperatures range 500–700 °C [ 52 ]. They demonstrate exceptionally good combinations of high hardness, high tensile and specific tensile strength values, keeping tensile ductility values up to 10% and more, which is considered acceptable for many engineering applications. They also exhibit deformation-induced phase transformations, including reversible BCC ↔ FCC transitions under strain and annealing. Not far from them are the Fe 60 Co 15 Ni 15 Cr 10  and Fe 62 Co 14 Ni 14 Cr 10  (here, subscript digits denote atomic percentages) medium-entropy alloys developed and studied recently [ 53 ,  54 ]. Production of high-entropy alloys from alloy scraps was also suggested recently [ 55 ]. At the same time, one should not use too high Al content with Ni and Co because these elements tend to form a ordered cP2 phase instead of the solid-solution cI2 one. Figure 1 Schematic representation of the approach to the HEA region from a corner (for example, starting from an A-element-based alloy) of the phase diagram by alloying a hypothetical base component  A  with elements  B ,  C , and  D , illustrated as an A to HEA route in the concentration tetrahedron of the quaternary  A – B – C – D  system.

In this context, high-entropy alloys developed starting from Fe–Mn steels have attracted growing attention due to high content of Mn reaching 30 mass% and more, good mechanical performance suitable for engineering applications, easy microstructural tailoring through FCC + BCC phases, high original mechanical properties, carbide formation on aging and suitability for advanced processing routes such as thermomechanical treatments.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: These new corner-approach HEAs demonstrate exceptionally high yield and ultimate strength values, which are superior to many other classical nearly equiatomic HEAs [ 56 ] (Fig.  2 a and Tables  S1  and  S2 ), yet having sufficiently large elongation. High Al content alloys containing hard BCC (cI2) and hard intermetallic compounds showed exceptionally high compressive strength over 2 GPa but only in compression [ 55 ], and presumably, they are brittle in tension. Large atomic size differences between the smaller Fe, Co, and Ni atoms and the larger Mn and Al atoms generate strong lattice distortion fields that hinder dislocation glide and enhance strength through solid-solution hardening. Recently developed eutectic high-entropy Ni-rich alloy (EHEA) of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition in different processing states [ 57 ] also showed reasonable high but still lower strength values (Fig.  2 a). In parallel, the Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C system alloy series show that industrial thermomechanical processing routes alone (homogenization, forging, rolling, aging) can induce tensile yield strengths up to 1.5–2.2 GPa (Fig.  2 a) with meaningful tensile ductility of 2–20%, without brittle intermetallic formation [ 58 ]. These properties are superior to those of other materials and close to those of martensitic and maraging steels [ 38 ,  59 ]. This also demonstrates that high-performance CA-HEAs can be produced via scalable metallurgical routes. Figure 2 a  Tensile strength of various HEAs and their elongation to failure. Hardness-to-strength relationships of the CA-HEAs and their fitting with linear  b  and power functions  c . Data from Tables  S1  and  S2 .

Moreover, these CA-HEAs demonstrate high specific strength values in the hot and cold rolled as well as hot, then cold-rolled and annealed states (Fig.  3 ). The DH1 crystal-metallic glass composite has a higher specific strength, but it demonstrates necking immediately after yielding, while the Ti–6Al–4V alloy has much lower strength compared to the CA-HEAs. The Fe–30Mn–10Co–9Al–0.8C (a typical notation in mass%, marked as Co10) (or Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 8.4 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1  in the atomic percent) samples processed by HPT show the highest strength and specific strength values. Note that in the atomic percents, all of these CA-HEAs have Fe content below 50%, yet they are solid-solution-type alloys with no intermetallic compounds. Classical HEAs located at the centers of the corresponding phase diagrams show much lower tensile strength and specific tensile strength (STS) values. A nearly linear  σ max -STS relationship is found owing to their similar densities close to 8. Figure 3 a  Ultimate tensile strength ( σ max ) of CA-HEAs, classical HEAs (blue rhombs) and typical industrial alloys in relation to their specific tensile strength values. Violet circular symbols are used for the stainless steel SUS304, ASTM A579 alloyed steel (A579), Al–Zn–Mg–Cu (Al-7075), Ti–6Al–4V, Fe–20Mn–11Al–1.8C–5Cr (Cr5), Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni (HSSS) alloys, classical Cantor HEA and Al 0.5 CoCrCuFeNi (Cantor-Al) HEAs, Zr 36.6 Ti 31.4 Nb 7 Cu 5.9 Be 19.1  (DH1) metallic glass–beta Ti phase composite, while red squares indicate the values of the Fe–30Mn–10Co–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 8.4 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 ) (Co10) CA-HEA in the following states: HPT—after high-pressure torsion with different strain values; HCR—hot and cold rolled; HCRA—hot, cold rolled and annealed. The data are taken from Refs [ 46 ,  58 ,  59 ,  65 ] and Tables  S1  and  S2 .  b  Tensile strength of CA-HEAs and some classical alloys in relation to their tensile elongation (from 4% and more). The data are taken from the same sources.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) such as high-pressure torsion (HPT) [ 61 ,  62 ] applied to conventional HEAs [ 63 ,  64 ] and the Fe–Mn–Co–Al–C medium- and high-entropy alloys with a duplex FCC + BCC microstructure reduces grain sizes to 50–100 nm (FCC grains being smaller than the BCC ones) and creates ultrahigh dislocation densities. After processing, the alloys reached hardness values of up to ~ 600 HV and demonstrated outstanding mechanical performance, with yield and ultimate tensile strengths exceeding 2 GPa while maintaining elongation to failure of up to 30% (see Fig.  3  and Table  S1 ) [ 65 ]. This breaks the conventional strength–ductility trade-off through hierarchical microstructural organization rather than phase hardening alone. Subsequent short-term aging introduced additional hardening to 700–800 HV, attributed to polygonization, possible formation of carbon atmospheres, and partial phase ordering, without any evidence of carbide precipitation. The ability to achieve ultrahigh strength together with good ductility through microstructural engineering via severe plastic deformation highlights the strong potential of these alloys for advanced structural applications. Recrystallization annealing helps to improve the tensile plasticity, keeping ultrahigh strength above 2 GPa. Positive effect of recrystallization annealing was also mentioned in other works [ 66 ].

sections.heading: Deformation energy storage
paragraphs:
Due to its high strain-hardening ability, an Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C system alloy exhibited a recovery and recrystallization heat of 1.05 kJ/mol after cold rolling, which is very high for cold-rolled materials. This exceeds the values reported for pure Fe (494 J/mol after 80% rolling [ 67 ]) and low-alloy steel (540 J/mol after 95% ECAP and rolling [ 68 ]), though it remains below that of Fe–Mn–C steel processed by high-pressure torsion [ 69 ]. Upon rapid heating to 650 °C (within ~ 12 min), 7.7 kJ/mol of energy is released in the Fe–30Mn–10Co–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 8.4 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 ) alloy processed by HPT before carbide precipitation occurs [ 65 ]. The exceptionally high stored energy detected by differential scanning calorimetry indicates a high density of lattice defects and their recovery during annealing. A similarly high value of 6.5 kJ/mol was obtained for the Fe–30Mn–20Co–9Al–0.8C (Al 19.7 C 3.1 Co 14.8 Fe 34.4 Mn 28.1 ) alloy having only 40.2 mass% and 34.4 at% Fe (Fig.  4 ). This suggests that such alloys could be promising for energy-related applications, where controlled release of stored energy is required. In the present systems, a large amount of energy is stored during deformation in the form of high defect density, refined microstructure, and metastable phases, including strain-induced phase transformations. It is shown that this stored energy can be partially recovered during subsequent annealing, indicating a reversible energy-storage mechanism. This behavior is similar to that observed in materials with reversible structural transformations, where energy introduced during deformation is released upon heating. Therefore, these alloys may be suitable for applications such as energy absorption systems where both high energy-absorption capacity and controlled release are required. Figure 4 DSC profile (heat flow  dQ/dt  versus temperature) of the Fe-30Mn-20Co-9Al-0.8C
(Al 19.7 C 3.1 Co 14.8 Fe 34.4 Mn 28.1 ) alloy sample after HPT processing with 4 full rotations tested
at a heating rate of 60 °C/min.

The surface structure of the FeMnCrCoNi HEA was successfully modified by shot peening [ 70 ]. Ultrasonic shot peening (USSP) produces  gradient structures in the FeMnCrCoNi HEA [ 71 ,  72 ] and Fe–Cr–Co–Ni MEAs by driving either defect accumulation or defect reorganization [ 73 ]. In annealed alloys, it induces grain refinement at the surface layer (Fig.  5 a), accumulation of dislocations, twinning (Fig.  5 b), and martensitic transformation (Fe 60 Co 15 Ni 15 Cr 10  alloy), leading to strong surface hardening, while in the pre-deformed state (by cold rolling), it promotes defect annihilation and mechanical softening despite surface hardening [ 73 ]. Phase stability and transformation behavior are composition-dependent, governed by stacking-fault energy and OSEC. These results show that USSP enables hierarchical structural and phase gradients, but its mechanical effects depend critically on alloy chemistry and processing history, providing a route for optimizing strength–ductility balance in advanced alloys. Figure 5 Dark-field  a  and HR HAADF STEM  b  images of the annealed Fe 60 Co 15 Ni 15 Cr 10  alloy sample after USSP treatment. The dashed line represents a boundary of the surface structure with nanograins. Reproduced from [ 73 ] with permission of Elsevier.

sections.heading: Structure
paragraphs: The Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C family alloys with good tensile properties form a major FCC phase, which is stabilized by high Mn and C content and a minor BCC one in many HEAs (Figs.  6  and  7 ). A minor BCC phase, present in these alloys, is stabilized by Al and Co, which can also form an ordered cP2 structure when the Al content is moderate–high. Al increases the stacking-fault energy (SFE) but simultaneously promotes B2/cP2 ordering of the initial cI2 BCC, as it is found in some HEAs [ 74 ]. A duplex FCC + BCC structure is observed at high Co content. As well as in the case of Cantor alloy, after cold rolling, the cF4 phase has a high density of dislocations, develops a dominant {110} < 110 > texture, typical of Brass-type rolling–recrystallization textures, and largely retains it after partial transformation upon annealing. In contrast, the restored cI2 phase exhibited a dominant {112} < 112 > texture. Figure 6 SEM images of the Fe–30Mn–10Co–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 8.4 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 ) alloy in as-cast  a  and hot and cold-rolled  b  state, secondary electrons. The bright (major) phase is FCC, while the dark one is BCC. Reproduced from [ 46 ] with permission of Springer Nature. Figure 7 Bright-field  a ,  c ,  e  TEM images and SAED patterns  b ,  d ,  f  of the Fe–30Mn–10Co–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 8.4 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 ) alloy sample in a cold-rolled state (50% reduction): cF4/FCC phase  a ,  b  and cI2/BCC one  c ,  d . cF4 phase with two twinned sub-grains with [110] zone axis  e ,  f  in a heavily strained area. SAED  f  is obtained from a twinned area in  e . MB indicates microbands (shear bands), TW indicates twins in  e . Partly reproduced from [ 46 ] with permission of Springer Nature.

The careful manipulation of the composition of these alloys leads to rich plasticity mechanisms: twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) [ 75 ,  76 ] in FCC grains (Fig.  7 e, f) and dislocation slip in these system alloys.

Another major conceptual advance is the controlled use of Cu as an alloying element [ 57 ,  77 ]. Traditionally considered detrimental in steels due to phase separation and hot shortness, Cu is here shown to enable excellent mechanical properties [ 78 ], enhanced corrosion and oxidation resistance [ 46 , 48 ], and novel duplex-phase structure. This reframes Cu from an impurity element into a microstructural design component in multicomponent alloys.

sections.heading: Heat treatment and low-temperature hardening
paragraphs: On long-term aging at 500–600 °C the FCC phase tends to form  κ -carbide (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC used for precipitation strengthening of these alloys [ 79 ], but rather surprisingly low-temperature aging at 200–300 °C led to much more significant and quick hardening and strengthening of the Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C system alloy (Fig.  8 ), which was not associated with nanoscale precipitates. Its microstructure is very similar to that of the cold-rolled one with a high density of dislocations, and no other diffraction rings/spots are found in FCC grains (Fig.  9 ), though polygonization forming small-angle boundaries is observed. Therefore, it is likely to be either short-range ordering prior to carbide precipitation or formation of the C atmospheres at dislocations. For example, chemically modulated mesoscopic domains suggesting short- and medium-range ordering (SRO and MRO, respectively) were observed in the CrMnFeCoNi equiatomic HEA [ 80 ] and Fe 40 Mn 40 Cr 10 Co 10  [ 81 ]. In the Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C system alloys, chemical ordering tendencies exist between Mn–Al, Mn–C, and Fe–C pairs, especially during thermomechanical processing. Figure 8 Vickers microhardness (HV) of the Fe–30Mn–5Co–3Ni–2Cu–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 4.4 Cu 2.0 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 Ni 2.0 ) alloy as a function of the annealing time and temperature (as indicated) after cold rolling. Reproduced from [ 58 ] with permission of Elsevier. Figure 9 Bright-field  a  and dark-field  b  TEM images and a SAED pattern with a large selective diaphragm (inset in  a ) of the Fe–30Mn–5Co–3Ni–2Cu–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 4.4 Cu 2.0 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 Ni 2.0 ) alloy annealed at 300 °C for 30 min after cold rolling (for 92%). The dark-field image was obtained using the (111) reflection. Reproduced from [ 58 ] with permission of Elsevier. High dislocation densities are still observed.

The Fe–30Mn–5Co–3Ni–2Cu–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 4.4 Cu 2.0 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 Ni 2.0 ) alloy, after severe cold rolling, exhibited a highly distorted FCC microstructure with extremely high dislocation density, fine elongated cellular structures, and significant misorientation between neighboring regions. Following low-temperature annealing at 300 °C for 30 min, the microstructure shows signs of recovery, including partial rearrangement of dislocations into more ordered and more equiaxed low-angle subgrain boundaries and their modest coarsening, indicating reduced overall lattice distortion. Surprisingly, this treatment resulted in substantial strengthening, an increase in hardness by about 50 HV and yield strength by nearly 200 MPa, rather than the expected softening from recovery. This counterintuitive hardening is attributed to the short-range ordering, or the formation of atmospheres of C on dislocations, which generate strain and strongly impede dislocation motion, outweighing any dislocation annihilation effects. The alloy with the high prior deformation, enhancing diffusion pathways through defects and generating crystal nucleation sites, enables this rapid low-temperature  response, making it a promising approach for achieving ultrahigh strength without high-temperature processing.

sections.heading: Strain-induced phase transformations
paragraphs: The strain-induced transformation of FCC austenite into BCC or body-centered tetragonal (BCT) structures in steels is commonly referred to as a strain-induced martensitic transformation [ 43 ,  45 ]. This phenomenon is often observed in certain metastable austenitic stainless steels and low-alloy steels and leads to TRIP effects. In contrast, the reverse transformation from the BCC structure to the FCC structure has rarely been reported. One of the strongest advantages of 3dLTM-based HEAs is their ability to respond strongly to mechanical processing. Deformation leads to reversible BCC → FCC transformation with subsequent thermal recovery (unique to Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C system alloys) (Fig.  10 ). Strain-induced and thermally reversible BCC → FCC transformation in Fe–Mn–Co–Ni–Cu–Al–C during heavy deformation are followed by a thermally reversible FCC → BCC recovery during annealing [ 58 ]. This is not common in HEAs, where usually FCC transforms to BCC or HCP martensitic structures [ 82 ]. In the Fe-30Mn-5Co-3Ni-2Cu-9Al-0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 4.4 Cu 2.0 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 Ni 2.0 ) alloy, deformation up to 92% strain leads to a partial BCC transformation, which is particularly notable because this alloy nominally stabilizes the FCC phase at room temperature. Such a transformation suggests a very low chemical driving force separating the two structures, consistent with the predictions of low free-energy differences between FCC and BCC in the Fe–Mn–Al–C system alloys [ 83 ]. The reverse transformation from BCC back to FCC upon heating to 600 °C supports the dynamic and reversible nature of the underlying phase instability. The magnetization of the cold-rolled sample after annealing at 600 °C for 2 h is about 3 times higher than that of the cold-rolled sample, in accordance with a higher fraction of the ferromagnetic BCC phase. Moreover, the linearity of the H-M curve of the cold-rolled sample resembles the paramagnetic behavior of the cF4 phase, while the H-M curve of the annealed one indicates the beginning of field saturation of the cI2 phase [ 58 ]. Figure 10 Bright-field TEM image  a , SAED pattern  b  and two dark-field images  c ,  d  of the Fe–30Mn–5Co–3Ni–2Cu–9Al–0.8C (Al 16.6 C 3.3 Co 4.4 Cu 2.0 Fe 44.6 Mn 27.1 Ni 2.0 ) alloy in a cold-rolled state. There are two sets of reflections in the SAED pattern representing the matrix cI2 (strong reflections with high-index [521] zone axis) and the transformed cF4 (weak reflections with [211] zone axis) phases. The dark-field images  c ,  d  were obtained in the reflections belonging to cF4 and cI2 phases, respectively. Reproduced from [ 58 ] with permission of Elsevier. Martensitic plates of the FCC phase are seen in  c .

During severe deformation, the BCC phase becomes thermodynamically destabilized relative to FCC due to the accumulation of stored defect energy. Dislocation accumulation increases internal energy and thus the Gibbs free energy of the BCC phase, providing the principal thermodynamic driving force for the forward transformation. Local compositional fluctuations under plastic flow may also reduce the Gibbs free-energy difference Δ G  between BCC and FCC phases and lower the energy barrier preventing nucleation of martensite, triggering the structural change. Shear banding creates zones of intense shear that promote martensitic-like displacive transformations. Upon annealing at moderate temperature (600 °C), the metastable FCC phase reverts to the thermodynamically stable BCC phase. This pronounced reversibility indicates a small transformation enthalpy difference.

sections.heading: Principles of the construction of CA-HEAs.
paragraphs: The proposed concept for developing high- and medium-entropy alloys from the corner of a phase diagram represents an evolutionary pathway from classical steels to MEA and HEA. It is built on the integrated control of chemical composition, microstructure, phase stability, and different strengthening mechanisms (Fig.  11 ). Figure 11 The principles for the creation of CA-HEAs.

The Fe–Mn–Al–C base system provides good phase tunability through structural variability, with FCC and BCC phases (by Mn, Ni, and C promoting FCC; by Al, Co, and Cr promoting BCC and its tendency to order into the cP2 structure). It allows fine adjustment of solid-solution strengthening (all additions), oxidation resistance (Cu), corrosion resistance (Cr), and defect pinning via stacking-fault energy control and local ordering. The properties are improved by achieving the balanced structural state (Fig.  11 ).

At the microstructural level, the strategy emphasizes the duplex-phase configurations, small-angle grain boundaries, nanocrystalline structures (using severe cold rolling and HPT), gradient structures (using USSP) and double FCC1/FCC2 structures. These architectures activate a synergistic spectrum of strengthening mechanisms: solid-solution strengthening, defect hardening, grain-size reduction strengthening, dispersion strengthening, local-ordering hardening, and transformation-mediated plastification by TRIP/TWIP-like effects. Significant hardening without classical carbide precipitation, likely from carbon atmospheres and partial ordering, highlights new strengthening paradigms to preserve ductility while achieving extreme strength levels.

Processing pathways integrate conventional metallurgical routes (casting, forging, hot and cold rolling) with severe plastic deformation techniques (severe cold rolling, HPT, USSP). Well-defined thermal treatment processes across a wide temperature window (low-temperature aging and recovery, medium-temperature polygonization, and high-temperature annealing/recrystallization) are combined with controlled phase transformations. This design framework enables the rational engineering of multiphase and hierarchically structured HEA/MEA materials with targeted strength–ductility balance leading to the development of structural materials for next-generation structural applications with ultrahigh strength values (> 2 GPa) and tensile ductility.

Conventional thermomechanical processing routes further demonstrate that these high-performance materials are not restricted to laboratory-scale processing. Industrial  forging, rolling, and aging treatments yield alloys with gigapascal-level strengths and tensile ductility.

sections.heading: Challenges, conflicting results and future research directions
paragraphs: Despite the rapid growth of HEA research activities in the scientific community, several challenges remain. One key problem is the unusual and still insufficiently understood phase transformation, especially the unusual strain-induced BCC to FCC transition and its reversible behavior during subsequent annealing.

Another challenge is the role of chemical heterogeneity at the nanoscale. Even when the alloy appears homogeneous, short-range order and local fluctuations may strongly affect phase stability and mechanical properties. One need is the development of strategies for the precise control of nanoscale heterogeneity, as compositionally complex HEAs naturally tend to develop compositional fluctuations.

The coupling between different deformation mechanisms, such as dislocation slip, twinning, and phase transformation, requires more attention, and it is challenging to predict which mechanism will dominate.

Future research directions include targeted nanoparticle inclusion and the controlled formation of SRO as design tools for microstructural engineering. Advanced characterization techniques, particularly atom probe tomography and in situ TEM, will be essential for revealing how SRO evolves during aging and deformation and how it contributes to strengthening mechanisms. At the same time, bridging atomistic simulations with experimental studies will be crucial for elucidating the mechanisms of deformation-induced phase transformations. The relatively high cost of the alloying elements compared to Fe indicates the necessity of searching for special applications where the HEA alloys’ properties are unique. For example, improvement of high-temperature phase stability, creep properties, and oxidation resistance represents promising directions for designing new HEAs for elevated-temperature structural applications.

In addition, carbon plays a complex role as an interstitial element, influencing phase stability, stacking-fault energy, and possible formation of atmospheres or precipitates. The origin of the excellent combination of high strength and good ductility, especially after severe plastic deformation, remains not fully resolved and challenges the classical strength–ductility relationship. There are also open questions about diffusion and kinetics in these alloys, as the idea of sluggish diffusion is still debated.

Finally, a major challenge is the lack of fully predictive models that can link composition, microstructure, and properties. Overall, these alloys could be considered as systems with strong spatial fluctuations, and their understanding may provide a new way to design advanced materials.

Another important issue is the presence of conflicting results reported in the literature. For example, diffusion in HEAs is often described as sluggish, while other studies report normal diffusion rates. Similarly, some works suggest the formation of stable solid solutions, whereas others observe chemical ordering or phase separation. The dominant deformation mechanisms also vary between studies, with reports of twinning-induced plasticity, transformation-induced plasticity, or dislocation slip depending on composition and processing history. In addition, the formation of precipitates such as carbides or ordered phases is not consistently reported. These discrepancies indicate that the behavior of HEAs is highly sensitive to local chemistry, processing conditions, and microstructural state. Resolving these contradictions requires systematic studies that combine precise control of composition and processing with advanced characterization and modeling.
